measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement separates the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and domestic hot water (DHW) loop into independent hydronic systems, each served by dedicated boilers and pumping configurations. The primary heating loop operates at higher temperatures for space heating, the WSHP loop operates at lower temperatures, and the DHW system functions on a separate loop without hydraulic or control integration. This configuration increases system complexity and limits opportunities for load diversity, heat recovery, and coordinated temperature optimization. During shoulder seasons, independent loop operation can contribute to boiler short cycling, elevated supply temperatures, and reduced overall plant efficiency.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and Hydronic Loop Reconfiguration (Primary loop + WSHP loop + DHW loop)
measures.notes: Reconfigure Primary heating loop, WSHP loop and DHW loop to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to evaluate reconfiguring the WSHP loop, primary heating loop, and DHW piping into a coordinated Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. Under a P-S configuration, a central boiler primary loop would maintain controlled supply temperatures while secondary loops draw only the required flow and temperature for each load. This arrangement provides hydraulic separation, allows differentiated temperature control for high- and low-temperature systems, improves outdoor-air reset effectiveness, and reduces short cycling. Improved integration may also enhance return-water temperature control, supporting more efficient boiler operation. When implemented in conjunction with condensing boiler upgrades, this redesign may allow optimization of boiler staging and potential reduction in total boiler count, thereby lowering long-term maintenance complexity and operating costs. Further engineering review is required to confirm detailed hydraulic configuration, load diversity assumptions, and control sequencing strategy.

measures.existing_conditions:
The existing heating boilers in the mechanical room are non-condensing, gas-fired Raypak units installed in 2006, with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately 78%. These boilers are approaching the end of their expected service life. As non-condensing equipment, they operate with higher flue-gas temperatures and cannot recover latent heat from combustion, resulting in reduced overall efficiency compared to modern condensing boiler technologies.
The boilers also lack advanced control features such as outdoor temperature reset and real-time modulation optimization. This limited control capability contributes to frequent short cycling and increased natural gas consumption. As a result, the system experiences elevated utility costs and higher greenhouse gas emissions.
While the boilers remain operational, their age and outdated design increase the likelihood of performance issues and rising maintenance requirements. Continued operation represents a missed opportunity for improved energy efficiency, lower operating costs, and enhanced reliability achievable through upgraded condensing boiler systems.
Retrofit Conditions
measures.notes: Replace existing non-condensing boiler to condensing boiler. Improves thermal efficiency, reduces natural gas consumption and lowers greenhouse gas emissions.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended that the existing non-condensing boilers be replaced with high-efficiency condensing boilers. Condensing boilers are designed to extract additional heat from the flue gases by recovering latent heat through a secondary heat exchanger, allowing them to achieve thermal efficiencies of up to 98%. This upgrade would substantially reduce natural gas consumption, lower utility costs, and improve overall system performance.
Modern condensing boilers also provide advanced control capabilities, including high-turndown modulation, integrated sequencing, and seamless compatibility with Building Automation Systems (BAS). These features improve load matching, reduce equipment cycling, and enhance operational reliability.
Upgrading to condensing boiler technology not only increases energy efficiency and reduces ongoing operating costs but also supports long-term sustainability objectives and contributes to meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

measures.measure_title: MUA Retrofit Two (2) Option: Hydronic MUA with VFD / WSHP MUA with VFD
measures.notes: Upgrade the existing MUA system by adding VFD control and converting to either a hydronic or water-source heat pump configuration to improve energy efficiency. Qualify for Enbridge incentives.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Option 1 – Install VFDs and Convert existing MUA to Hydronic MUA
Mann recommends installing a new hydronic heating coil in the existing make-up air (MUA) unit, to be served by the central boiler plant. A modulating control valve would regulate heating-water flow to maintain corridor supply-air temperature.
As the existing MUA unit is currently operating without VFD control, new variable-frequency drives (VFDs) should be installed on the supply fan to enable proper airflow modulation. Once installed, the VFDs will be fully integrated into the BAS to provide optimized fan control, scheduling, and occupancy-based ventilation reduction.
Hydronic conversion also reduces maintenance requirements and qualifies for Enbridge incentives, improving overall project payback.

Option 2 – Install VFDs and Convert existing MUA to Water-Source Heat Pump (WSHP) MUA
Mann recommends converting the existing make-up air (MUA) unit to a water-source heat pump (WSHP) MUA unit. The new WSHP heating coil can be installed within the existing MUA cabinet, allowing the building to retain most of the original ventilation infrastructure. 
The existing WSHP loop piping can remain and be reused, and the boiler plant would continue to provide supplemental heat only when required. A WSHP-based heating coil is significantly more efficient than a gas-fired burner because it uses the thermal energy already present within the building—rather than generating heat through combustion. The WSHP coil is capable of providing heating whenever the ventilation system operates and can take advantage of heat already present in the hydronic loop, reducing boiler runtime and improving overall system efficiency. One consideration is that the MUA electrical load may increase slightly depending on the WSHP coil configuration; however, the improved efficiency and reduced gas usage often outweigh these impacts. 
During the heating season, the WSHP coil extracts heat from the hydronic loop and transfers it into the ventilation air stream. When more heat is required than is being generated within the building, the central boiler plant provides supplemental heat to maintain loop temperature. 
During warmer weather, suites operating in cooling mode can reject heat into the WSHP loop, supplying “free heat” to the MUA heating coil during mild outdoor conditions. During shoulder seasons, the system can recycle heat internally: heat removed from south-facing suites in cooling mode can offset ventilation heating demands from north-facing corridors, reducing the need for gas-fired heating entirely.

Where applicable, motion sensors may be integrated with existing lighting control strategies or future centralized control systems to further enhance operational flexibility.

measures.existing_conditions:
The domestic hot water (DHW) system is currently equipped with a FlowMix electronic thermostatic mixing valve to regulate DHW delivery temperature. While the valve provides temperature control functionality, electronic mixing valves typically require specialized troubleshooting, proprietary components, and manufacturer-specific service support.

On-site staff indicated that maintenance and repair costs for the existing electronic mixing valve are high, and servicing often requires calling specialized contractors rather than in-house maintenance personnel. This increases ongoing maintenance costs and can result in longer downtime when issues occur.
measures.measure_title: Replace Electronic Mixing Valve with Mechanical Thermostatic Mixing Valve
measures.notes: Replace existing Flowmix electric mixging valve with mechanical mixing valve when the unit end of its life. The proposed valve would maintain consistent and safe DHW delivery temperatures while improving system robustness and long-term maintainability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing electronic mixing valve with a standard mechanical thermostatic mixing valve when existing electric mixing valve end of its service life. A mechanical mixing valve provides reliable temperature control using a passive thermostatic element, without the need for electronic controls, sensors, or external power.

This retrofit would simplify DHW system operation, reduce long-term maintenance costs, and improve serviceability. Mechanical mixing valves can typically be adjusted, repaired, or replaced by building maintenance staff, reducing reliance on specialized service providers. 

*Further engineering review would be required to confirm valve sizing, temperature setpoints, and compatibility with the existing DHW storage and distribution system.

measures.notes: Replace existing Flowmix electric mixging valve with mechanical mixing valve when the unit end of its life. The proposed valve would maintain consistent and safe DHW delivery temperatures while improving system robustness and long-term maintainability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:

During warmer weather, suites operating in cooling mode can reject heat into the WSHP loop, supplying “free heat” to the MUA heating coil during mild outdoor conditions. During shoulder seasons, the system can recycle heat internally: heat removed from south-facing suites in cooling mode can offset ventilation heating demands from north-facing corridors, reducing the need for gas-fired heating entirely.
